riscos.descricao: Possível vazamento de dados por sobreposição entre dados de treino dos LLMs e de teste; o estudo considera a ameaça limitada com base em trabalho anterior [34] e na comparação de EM com modelos aprendidos.
A seleção de exemplos melhora pouco os erros de compilação e de execução, atribuídos pelo estudo a diferenças entre linguagens e à falta de conhecimento de bibliotecas de terceiros.
No estudo de caso, exemplos recuperados por similaridade lexical (LD) não trazem o conhecimento necessário e a tradução falha com IndexError na verificação de limite de string.
Dependência da base de exemplos: o desempenho da CAST cai com base menor e com ruído estrutural nos exemplos (embaralhamento de instruções).
Ameaças à validade declaradas: implementação das técnicas comparadas, qualidade do conjunto de dados e construção das métricas de avaliação.

mitigacoes.descricao: Comparação das taxas de EM dos LLMs com as de modelos aprendidos, apresentada como indício de vazamento mínimo, e remissão a trabalho anterior [34].
Uso do conjunto de dados limpo de [34], com verificação cruzada em pares por quatro autores.
Reuso das implementações e pesos dos modelos comparados.
Adoção de CA e EM para avaliar correção léxica e semântica.

citacoes.trecho: This paper employs in-context learning (ICL), which directly integrates task exemplars into the input context, to post-incorporate code structural knowledge into pre-trained LLMs.
Code translation migrates codebases across programming languages.

Besides, our CAST retrieval method includes two variants: 1) CAST-F: Selects a fixed number of exemplars based on the predefined capacity limit k. 2) CAST-A: Automatically determines the number of exemplars using a CAST (defined in Eq. (10)) threshold, allowing early stop when the coverage rate reaches the threshold.
Specifically, the Levenshtein Distance is employed to recall the top-⌊t · k⌋ nearest candidates.
The selected k exemplar translation pairs are directly concatenated with the test source code to create the prompt, as shown in Fig. 2.
You are a professional developer proficient in java and python.
Translate given java code to python code, and use END_OF_CASE to finish your answer:
Fixed Exemplars (Fixed): A static exemplar set is shared across all test samples:
Random Sampling (Random): k exemplars are uniformly sampled from the candidate pool
Retrieval by Levenshtein Distance (LD): The score is defined as the negative sum of Levenshtein distances between each exemplar and the test sample:

Similarly, the method Retrieval by AST Edit Distance (AST-ED) is defined based on the Tree Edit Distance [44] between each exemplar and the test sample, where only the type information of AST nodes is retained for distance calculation to improve generalization, aligning with the setting of CAST.
Retrieval by CodeBERT Similarity (CodeBERT): Each sample is encoded using a CodeBERT embedding function fCB(·), and cosine similarity is used:
Retrieval by BM25 (BM25): The score is the sum of BM25 relevance scores between each candidate and the test input:
Diversity with Clustering (Diversity): The candidate pool is clustered into k groups using CodeBERT embeddings, and the most similar sample in each cluster is selected:

For each pre-trained LLM, we use it to translate the entire test dataset and verify the predictions using test input cases. Samples that pass all test input cases are added to the database for this LLM. Models are evaluated on the remaining data, and final metrics are computed using the entire dataset, treating the database samples as exactly correct.
Of these, 568 include unit tests for at least one programming language: 464 for Python, 482 for Java, and 467 for C++.
The internal validity threat comes from potential LLM data leakage due to possible training/testing set overlaps, but prior work [34] shows this threat is limited.
Compared to learning-based methods, which ensure no data leakage during training, the EM scores of LLMs are comparable, indicating minimal data leakage.

ICL yields limited improvements for “Compile Error” and “Runtime Error.” These limitations likely stem from cross-language differences and the lack of comprehensive third-party library knowledge, which hinder LLMs’ ability to resolve such errors.

The case shows that the translated code fails in string boundary checking, resulting in an IndexError: string index out of range, where correctly translating this construct requires knowledge of the difference between C++ null-terminator-based string handling (’\0’) and Python’s length-based indexing (len()).
CAST performance degrades with reduced database size (2.93% drop at 25% sampling) and structural noise (2.81% loss with statement shuffle).
The first external validity threat is in the implementation of the compared techniques. To reduce it, we select state-of-the-art pre-trained models and reuse their implementations and weights.
We use the cleaned dataset from [34], where four authors cross-checked their cleaned results in pairs to reach a consensus for each group of parallel functions.
To reduce this threat, we adopt CA and EM to evaluate the code translation performance of different approaches from both lexical and semantic correctness as most of the relevant papers [31]–[34].
Specifically, the proprietary LLMs, such as GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini, achieve an average CA of 66.37% and 69.72%, respectively, indicating strong potential for LLM-based code translation.
Specifically, it surpasses the second-best strategy, Diversity, by 1.6% for Qwen2-7B, 1.9% for Gemma2-27B, and 1.14% for Qwen2.5-72B.
Specifically, CAST-F excels not only in BLEU and WNG but also in Syntactic and dataflow alignment, demonstrating its ability to capture both surface-level and structural aspects of code.
Additionally, for a fairer comparison, we evaluate CAST-F with 5-shots on Gemma2-(2B/9B/27B), all of which are from the same family.
We conduct t-tests comparing CAST-F with each other ICL retrieval strategies.
The replication package is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16920815.
